title: Vector Database Internals and Optimization
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Vector Database Internals and Optimization ##### 94% recall, and nobody knew A team in Chennai ran a RAG system over 8 million document chunks. Retrieval latency was excellent — p95 of 18ms. Answer quality was persistently mediocre and nobody could explain why. Someone finally built a brute-force exact-search index over a 50,000-chunk sample and compared results. Their HNSW index was returning **76% of the true top-10**. One in four correct chunks was simply never surfaced — not ranked low, not filtered out, just missed by the graph traversal. `ef_search` was at the library default of 40. On an 8-million-vector index with `M=16`, that is far too small a candidate list. They raised `ef_search` to 200. Recall went to 97.4%, latency went to 41ms, and answer quality improved by 11 points. **ANN search is approximate by definition, and almost nobody measures how approximate.** You cannot tune what you have not measured, and a recall number is the difference between an engineering decision and a hope. Day 34 introduced HNSW; today is the internals and the tuning. ##### HNSW internals Hierarchical Navigable Small World builds a layered proximity graph. Each layer is a navigable small-world graph; higher layers are sparser with longer-range links. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph L2["Layer 2 — sparse, long hops"] A2((" ")) --- B2((" ")) end subgraph L1["Layer 1"] A1((" ")) --- B1((" ")) --- C1((" ")) --- D1((" ")) end subgraph L0["Layer 0 — every vector, M links each"] A0((" ")) --- B0((" ")) --- C0((" ")) --- D0((" ")) --- E0((" ")) --- F0((" ")) end Q["query enters
at top"] --> A2 A2 -.descend.-> B1 B1 -.descend.-> C0 C0 --> R["ef_search candidates
→ return top k"] ``` **Insertion.** Each new vector is assigned a maximum layer drawn from an exponentially decaying distribution — `floor(-ln(uniform()) * mL)` where `mL = 1/ln(M)`. Most vectors land only in layer 0; roughly `1/M` reach layer 1, and so on. The vector is then connected to its `M` nearest neighbours in every layer it occupies, found by greedy search using `ef_construction` candidates. **Search.** Enter at the top layer's entry point, greedily walk toward the query until no neighbour is closer, descend, repeat. At layer 0, run a best-first search maintaining a dynamic candidate list of size `ef_search`, and return the top `k`. ```python import heapq import numpy as np def hnsw_layer0_search(graph, vectors, query, entry_point, ef, k): """Simplified layer-0 best-first search. Shows what ef_search controls.""" def dist(i): return -float(vectors[i] @ query) # negative cosine = distance visited = {entry_point} candidates = [(dist(entry_point), entry_point)] # min-heap results = [(-dist(entry_point), entry_point)] # max-heap of size ef while candidates: d, node = heapq.heappop(candidates) worst = -results[0][0] if d > worst and len(results) >= ef: break # nothing closer remains for neighbour in graph[node]: if neighbour in visited: continue visited.add(neighbour) nd = dist(neighbour) if nd < worst or len(results) < ef: heapq.heappush(candidates, (nd, neighbour)) heapq.heappush(results, (-nd, neighbour)) if len(results) > ef: heapq.heappop(results) # drop the worst worst = -results[0][0] return [n for _, n in sorted([(-d, n) for d, n in results])[:k]] ``` **Read the `break` condition.** The search stops when the nearest unexplored candidate is farther than the worst of your current `ef` results. A small `ef` terminates early, before the traversal has reached the region containing the true nearest neighbours — that is exactly the Chennai failure. **The parameters:** | Parameter | Controls | Typical | Effect of increasing | |---|---|---|---| | **`M`** | Links per node at layer 0 | 16–64 | Better recall, more memory, slower build | | **`ef_construction`** | Candidates during insertion | 100–500 | Better graph quality, much slower build | | **`ef_search`** | Candidates during query | 50–400 | **Better recall, slower query** | **`ef_search` is tunable at query time**, which is the practical lever. The same index can serve interactive queries at `ef=64` and an offline evaluation job at `ef=400`. **Memory:** ```python def hnsw_memory_gb(n_vectors, dims, M=16, dtype_bytes=4): vectors = n_vectors * dims * dtype_bytes # Layer 0 has 2M links; higher layers add ~M/(M-1) more on average links = n_vectors * (2 * M + M / (M - 1)) * 4 # 4-byte node ids return {"vectors_GB": round(vectors / 1e9, 2), "graph_GB": round(links / 1e9, 2), "total_GB": round((vectors + links) / 1e9, 2)} for M in [16, 32, 64]: print(f"M={M:>2}, 8M vectors, 768d:", hnsw_memory_gb(8_000_000, 768, M)) ``` ##### IVF and product quantization HNSW keeps everything in RAM. At hundreds of millions of vectors that stops being affordable, and IVF+PQ is the standard answer. **IVF (Inverted File Index)** partitions the space with k-means into `nlist` cells. At query time, search only the `nprobe` nearest cells. $$\text{cost} \approx \frac{n}{n_{\text{list}}} \times n_{\text{probe}} \quad \text{comparisons instead of } n$$ **Product Quantization** compresses each vector. Split a 768-dimensional vector into `m` sub-vectors, run k-means with 256 centroids in each sub-space, and store `m` bytes instead of 3,072. ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import KMeans class ProductQuantizer: """Split into m subspaces, quantize each to 256 centroids (1 byte).""" def __init__(self, m=96, n_centroids=256, seed=42): self.m, self.n_centroids, self.seed = m, n_centroids, seed self.codebooks = None def fit(self, vectors): n, d = vectors.shape assert d % self.m == 0, "dims must divide evenly into m subspaces" self.sub_dim = d // self.m self.codebooks = np.zeros((self.m, self.n_centroids, self.sub_dim), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(self.m): sub = vectors[:, i * self.sub_dim:(i + 1) * self.sub_dim] km = KMeans(n_clusters=self.n_centroids, n_init=3, random_state=self.seed).fit(sub) self.codebooks[i] = km.cluster_centers_ return self def encode(self, vectors): n = vectors.shape[0] codes = np.zeros((n, self.m), dtype=np.uint8) for i in range(self.m): sub = vectors[:, i * self.sub_dim:(i + 1) * self.sub_dim] d = ((sub[:, None, :] - self.codebooks[i][None]) ** 2).sum(-1) codes[:, i] = d.argmin(1) return codes def asymmetric_distance_table(self, query): """Precompute query-to-centroid distances; then scoring is table lookups.""" table = np.zeros((self.m, self.n_centroids), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(self.m): q_sub = query[i * self.sub_dim:(i + 1) * self.sub_dim] table[i] = ((self.codebooks[i] - q_sub) ** 2).sum(-1) return table def search(self, query, codes, k=10): table = self.asymmetric_distance_table(query) dists = table[np.arange(self.m), codes].sum(axis=1) # vectorised lookup idx = np.argpartition(dists, k)[:k] return idx[np.argsort(dists[idx])] def compression_ratio(dims, m, dtype_bytes=4): return {"original_bytes": dims * dtype_bytes, "pq_bytes": m, "ratio": round(dims * dtype_bytes / m, 1)} print(compression_ratio(768, 96)) # 3072 → 96 bytes, 32× compression ``` **Asymmetric distance computation is the clever part.** The query stays in full precision; only the database vectors are quantized. Precompute a small `m × 256` table of query-to-centroid distances, and scoring any vector becomes `m` table lookups and a sum — no floating-point vector arithmetic at all. **IVF+PQ trade-offs:** 32× memory reduction, recall typically 85–95% (versus HNSW's 95–99%), and it requires a training step on a sample. Use it past roughly 50 million vectors, or when memory is the binding constraint. **`nlist` and `nprobe` guidance:** `nlist ≈ 4√n` is the standard heuristic — 4,000 cells for 1M vectors, 16,000 for 16M. `nprobe` between 8 and 64, tuned for recall exactly as `ef_search` is. ##### Index selection ```mermaid flowchart TD A["How many vectors?"] --> B{"< 50k"} B -->|Yes| C["Flat / brute force
exact, no tuning"] B -->|No| D{"< 10M?"} D -->|Yes| E{"Memory available?"} E -->|Ample| F["HNSW
best recall/latency"] E -->|Tight| G["IVF-Flat or
HNSW + int8"] D -->|"10M - 500M"| H{"Recall critical?"} H -->|Yes| I["HNSW + PQ
or IVF-PQ, high nprobe"] H -->|No| J["IVF-PQ"] D -->|"> 500M"| K["IVF-PQ, sharded
or DiskANN"] ``` | Index | Recall | Query | Memory | Build | Use | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Flat | 1.00 | O(n) | 1× | None | < 50k, or ground truth | | **HNSW** | 0.95–0.99 | O(log n) | 1.3–2× | Slow | **< 50M, the default** | | IVF-Flat | 0.90–0.98 | O(n·np/nl) | 1.05× | Fast | Medium, memory-tight | | **IVF-PQ** | 0.85–0.95 | Very fast | **0.03×** | Moderate | **> 50M** | | HNSW-PQ | 0.88–0.96 | Fast | 0.05× | Slow | Large + latency-sensitive | | DiskANN | 0.90–0.96 | ~1ms (SSD) | Disk-based | Very slow | Billions, cost-sensitive | ##### Measuring recall The step the Chennai team skipped for eight months. ```python import numpy as np import time def build_ground_truth(vectors, queries, k=10, batch=256): """Exact top-k by brute force. This is your reference.""" truth = [] for i in range(0, len(queries), batch): q = queries[i:i + batch] sims = q @ vectors.T # assumes normalised idx = np.argpartition(-sims, k, axis=1)[:, :k] rows = np.arange(len(q))[:, None] order = np.argsort(-sims[rows, idx], axis=1) truth.append(idx[rows, order]) return np.vstack(truth) def measure_recall(index_search_fn, queries, ground_truth, k=10): """recall@k = |returned ∩ true_topk| / k, plus latency percentiles.""" recalls, latencies = [], [] for q, truth in zip(queries, ground_truth): t0 = time.perf_counter() returned = index_search_fn(q, k) latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) recalls.append(len(set(returned) & set(truth[:k])) / k) return { f"recall@{k}": round(float(np.mean(recalls)), 4), "recall_p10": round(float(np.percentile(recalls, 10)), 4), "p50_ms": round(float(np.percentile(latencies, 50)), 2), "p95_ms": round(float(np.percentile(latencies, 95)), 2), "qps": round(1000 / float(np.mean(latencies)), 1), } ``` **`recall_p10` matters as much as the mean.** A mean recall of 0.94 with a p10 of 0.60 means one query in ten is badly served — and those are disproportionately the hard, important queries. **Sample if the corpus is large.** Ground truth over 8 million vectors is expensive; build it over a 200,000-vector sample with 500 queries. The recall estimate transfers. ##### The recall-latency curve Your practical task, and the artefact every retrieval system should have. ```python import faiss import numpy as np def sweep_hnsw(vectors, queries, ground_truth, M_values=(16, 32, 64), ef_search_values=(16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512), k=10, ef_construction=200): """Build at each M, sweep ef_search, record recall and latency.""" d = vectors.shape[1] rows = [] for M in M_values: index = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, M, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT) index.hnsw.efConstruction = ef_construction t0 = time.perf_counter() index.add(vectors) build_s = time.perf_counter() - t0 for ef in ef_search_values: if ef < k: continue index.hnsw.efSearch = ef def search(q, kk): _, idx = index.search(q.reshape(1, -1).astype("float32"), kk) return idx[0].tolist() stats = measure_recall(search, queries, ground_truth, k) rows.append({"M": M, "ef_search": ef, "build_s": round(build_s, 1), **stats}) return rows ``` A representative sweep on 1M × 768d vectors: | M | ef_search | recall@10 | p95 ms | QPS | |---|---|---|---|---| | 16 | 32 | 0.812 | 1.4 | 892 | | 16 | 64 | 0.901 | 2.1 | 604 | | 16 | 128 | 0.954 | 3.6 | 351 | | 16 | 256 | 0.981 | 6.4 | 198 | | **32** | **128** | **0.977** | **4.1** | **312** | | 32 | 256 | 0.991 | 7.2 | 176 | | 64 | 128 | 0.988 | 5.8 | 218 | **Read the frontier, not the individual rows.** `M=32, ef=128` dominates `M=16, ef=256` — better recall *and* better latency, at the cost of more memory and a slower build. That kind of domination is common and only visible when you sweep both parameters. **Practical targets:** 0.95 recall for most RAG (the reranker recovers some misses), 0.99 for high-stakes retrieval, 0.90 acceptable when a strong reranker follows and latency is critical. ##### Filtering strategies Metadata filtering interacts badly with graph traversal, and the interaction is worth understanding. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Query + filter"] --> B{"Filter selectivity?"} B -->|"> 30% pass"| C["Post-filter:
search, then discard"] B -->|"5-30% pass"| D["Filtered traversal:
skip non-matching nodes
during search"] B -->|"< 5% pass"| E["Pre-filter:
gather matching ids,
brute force over them"] C --> F["Fast, may return < k"] D --> G["Best general approach"] E --> H["Exact, fast on small sets"] ``` **Post-filtering** searches normally then discards non-matching results. Simple, but with a 2% selective filter your top-100 may contain zero valid results. **Filtered traversal** — used by Qdrant and Weaviate — checks the filter during graph walking and skips non-matching nodes. It handles moderate selectivity well but can disconnect the graph when the filter is very restrictive, causing the search to terminate early with poor recall. **Pre-filtering** collects matching IDs first and brute-forces over them. Optimal below a few thousand candidates. ```python def adaptive_filtered_search(index, query, filter_dict, metadata_index, k=10, total_vectors=1_000_000): """Choose the filtering strategy by estimated selectivity.""" matching_ids = metadata_index.get_ids(filter_dict) selectivity = len(matching_ids) / total_vectors if selectivity < 0.05 or len(matching_ids) < 5000: return brute_force_over_subset(query, matching_ids, k) if selectivity > 0.30: raw = index.search(query, k=k * 4) # over-fetch return [r for r in raw if r["id"] in matching_ids][:k] return index.search_filtered(query, k=k, filter=filter_dict) ``` **Over-fetch when post-filtering.** Fetching `k*4` and filtering gives you a much better chance of returning a full `k` results. Some systems adapt the multiplier based on observed pass rates. **Partition by high-selectivity dimensions instead of filtering.** If every query filters by tenant, build one index per tenant. Filtering is then free, and each index is smaller and faster. ##### Sharding and replication ```python def shard_plan(n_vectors, dims, M=32, max_gb_per_shard=24, target_qps=500, qps_per_replica=300): mem = hnsw_memory_gb(n_vectors, dims, M) n_shards = max(1, int(np.ceil(mem["total_GB"] / max_gb_per_shard))) n_replicas = max(1, int(np.ceil(target_qps / qps_per_replica))) return { "total_index_GB": mem["total_GB"], "shards": n_shards, "vectors_per_shard": n_vectors // n_shards, "replicas_per_shard": n_replicas, "total_nodes": n_shards * n_replicas, "gb_per_node": round(mem["total_GB"] / n_shards, 1), } ``` **Sharding is for memory; replication is for throughput and availability.** They are independent axes and conflating them leads to over-provisioning. **Two sharding strategies:** - **Random** — query all shards, merge results. Uniform load, but every query touches every shard, so tail latency is the max across shards. - **Semantic or tenant-based** — route queries to relevant shards only. Much cheaper per query, but load can be uneven and cross-shard queries need a router. For multi-tenant products, **shard by tenant**. It gives you free filtering, isolation, and the ability to delete a tenant's data cleanly — which matters under DPDP Act erasure obligations. ##### Memory versus disk **DiskANN** (Microsoft) keeps the graph on SSD with a compressed in-memory index for navigation. Roughly 1ms latency at billion scale, at a fraction of the RAM cost. ```python def cost_comparison(n_vectors, dims, ram_inr_per_gb_month=380, ssd_inr_per_gb_month=9): hnsw = hnsw_memory_gb(n_vectors, dims, M=32)["total_GB"] ivfpq = n_vectors * 96 / 1e9 + n_vectors * dims * 4 / 1e9 * 0.02 diskann_ram = n_vectors * 32 / 1e9 # compressed navigation index diskann_disk = n_vectors * dims * 4 / 1e9 return { "hnsw_inr_month": round(hnsw * ram_inr_per_gb_month), "ivfpq_inr_month": round(ivfpq * ram_inr_per_gb_month), "diskann_inr_month": round(diskann_ram * ram_inr_per_gb_month + diskann_disk * ssd_inr_per_gb_month), } print(cost_comparison(100_000_000, 768)) ``` At 100 million vectors the difference between HNSW in RAM and DiskANN is roughly an order of magnitude in monthly cost. That arithmetic is what decides architecture at scale. ##### Common mistakes - **Never measuring recall against exact search** — the 76% that went unnoticed. - **Default `ef_search`** on a large index. - **Tuning `ef_search` without also trying higher `M`** — you may be on a dominated point. - **Post-filtering with a highly selective filter**, returning almost nothing. - **Not over-fetching** when post-filtering. - **`nlist` far from `4√n`**, giving cells that are too large or too small. - **IVF-PQ without training** on a representative sample. - **Reporting mean recall only**, hiding a bad p10. - **Sharding for throughput** when replication is what you need. - **HNSW at 200M vectors** when IVF-PQ would cost a tenth as much. - **Rebuilding the whole index** for incremental updates instead of using upserts and periodic compaction. - **Different metric at build and query time** — cosine versus L2 mismatches produce silently wrong results. ##### Hands-on: build ground truth first Your practical task tunes HNSW parameters and plots the recall-latency curve. **Build the exact ground truth before anything else** — without it you are tuning latency against nothing. Sweep both `M` and `ef_search`, plot recall on the y-axis against p95 latency on the x-axis, and mark the Pareto frontier. Then pick the point that meets your latency budget and note the recall you are accepting. The mini project benchmarks IVF+PQ against HNSW at 1M+ vectors on recall, latency, and memory. Use FAISS for both so the comparison is fair. Report peak RSS during the build and during queries, not just the theoretical index size — PQ's training step is memory-hungry and that surprises people. Sweep `nprobe` for IVF exactly as you swept `ef_search` for HNSW. The assignment writes a tuning guide for a chosen vector database. Make it operational: a table of index types by corpus size, the parameters that matter for each with starting values, the filtering strategy by selectivity, and the exact procedure for measuring recall. Include a worked example — "for 20M vectors at 768d with a 50ms budget, use HNSW with M=32, ef_construction=200, ef_search=96, expect recall 0.96 and 34 GB" — because that is what someone actually needs. ##### Key takeaways - **ANN is approximate and you must measure it.** Build exact ground truth on a sample and compute recall; a default `ef_search` on a large index can silently return 76% of the right answers. - **`ef_search` is tunable per query** — run interactive traffic at low `ef` and offline evaluation at high `ef` from the same index. - **Sweep `M` and `ef_search` together.** Higher `M` with moderate `ef` often dominates low `M` with high `ef` on both recall and latency. - **Match the filtering strategy to selectivity**: pre-filter below 5%, filtered traversal in the middle, post-filter with over-fetch above 30% — and partition by tenant when you can. - **IVF-PQ gives 32× memory reduction** for a few points of recall, which is the difference between affordable and not past roughly 50 million vectors.
